current_citation_section: 1. Introduction | 2.1. Image-informed compression-after-impact strength assessment | 4.1. Paired images, mechanical labels and evaluation units
current_citation_context: B005: Compression-after-impact (CAI) strength connects the observed damage of a composite laminate to its residual compressive capacity. For carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer laminates, surface images and internal C-scan images provide complementary descriptions of the impacted specimen. Public paired-image datasets and measured CAI labels make this connection accessible to data-driven assessment [1, 2]. Image-based regression has further shown how C-scan spatial information can support strength prediction [3]. These developments create an opportunity to improve not only the predictor, but also the observations supplied to it. | B014: Image-informed strength assessment learns the relationship between an observed damage state and the subsequent mechanical response. Hasebe and colleagues released paired surface and internal-damage images after impact, together with subsequent CAI measurements [1, 2]. These resources support specimen-level investigation of complementary image modalities: the surface describes externally visible morphology, while C-scan images provide a spatial description of internal damage. Their pairing with mechanical labels makes it possible to evaluate how the supplied image information contributes to quantitative strength estimation. | B083: The study uses publicly released surface and internal-damage images of impacted carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer laminates, paired with measured CAI strength [1, 2, 9]. The assembled cohort contains 276 physical specimens from six source groups covering cross-ply and quasi-isotropic layups with 8, 16 and 24 layers. Each record connects a specimen identifier, a registered image pair and a mechanical label in MPa. Regional acquisition is evaluated through offline revelation of the two-dimensional C-scan raster; the strength labels are the source authors' mechanical measurements.

current_citation_context: B005: Compression-after-impact (CAI) strength connects the observed damage of a composite laminate to its residual compressive capacity. For carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer laminates, surface images and internal C-scan images provide complementary descriptions of the impacted specimen. Public paired-image datasets and measured CAI labels make this connection accessible to data-driven assessment [1, 2]. Image-based regression has further shown how C-scan spatial information can support strength prediction [3]. These developments create an opportunity to improve not only the predictor, but also the observations supplied to it. | B015: Mack and colleagues used a ResNet18-based model to predict impact energy and CAI strength from C-scan images [3]. This work establishes a close engineering precedent for learning image-to-strength relationships. We extend the assessment question from reading available image content to selecting the regional content that becomes available during prediction. A common strength predictor provides the readout for this comparison, so the evaluated change is the organization of its observations. Final accuracy describes the selected content at completion, and the prediction trajectory describes its usefulness as acquisition progresses. | B153: This formulation extends image-informed CAI regression [3] by optimizing the input sequence as well as evaluating its readout. It also connects the observation--update--decision structure of autonomous inspection [4] and active feature acquisition [5, 6] to a continuous strength trajectory. The common-predictor design attributes the evaluated difference to the complete selection mechanism. Surface conditioning, observed internal content, history and global task state operate together in that mechanism; their separate contributions would require matched component interventions. Similarly, the fixed-set experiment evaluates arrival within the selected content, rather than assigning additive percentages of the total gain to selection and order.
